notes.meaning: After David settled his kingdom, he asked if anyone from Saul's family was still alive. In the ancient world, a new king usually wiped out the previous ruler's family to prevent rebellions. David did the exact opposite because he remembered the solemn covenant of friendship he had made with Jonathan.

Royal officials found a man named Ziba, who had served as a manager in Saul's household. When called into David's presence, Ziba acknowledged the king and presented himself as David's servant. Because Ziba knew the private affairs of Saul's family, he was able to provide the answers David needed.

David asked specifically to show the 'kindness of God,' meaning an extraordinary mercy that mirrors God's own faithful love. Ziba replied that Jonathan had a surviving son who was disabled in both feet from a childhood fall. David did not let the young man's physical disability stop him from extending royal favor.

David immediately asked where the young man could be found. Ziba explained that he was living east of the Jordan River in Lo-debar at the home of Machir. Having lost his family lands, Jonathan's son lived quietly as a dependent guest in someone else's house.

David promptly sent messengers to bring Jonathan's son to the royal palace. Machir had shown noble generosity in sheltering the prince, and David now provided the transportation he needed to travel. Instead of summoning someone to wait on him, the king sent for someone he could bless.

Mephibosheth arrived before David and bowed face down to the floor in deep reverence. Because he was a crippled descendant of the former royal family, he likely feared he was being brought to his death. David spoke his name gently to put his fears to rest.

David told Mephibosheth not to fear, promising him steadfast kindness for the sake of his father Jonathan. The king restored all the private land that had once belonged to Saul's family. In addition, David granted Mephibosheth the high honor of dining regularly at the royal table as the king's permanent guest.

Mephibosheth bowed down again, overwhelmed by such unexpected favor. He referred to himself as a 'dead dog,' a common ancient phrase describing someone lowly, powerless, and utterly unworthy of attention. He knew he had done nothing to earn such royal grace.

David called Ziba into the room to give him official instructions. The king formally announced that Saul's entire family estate was now transferred to Mephibosheth. This decree instantly lifted Jonathan's son out of poverty and restored his family's wealth.

David commanded Ziba, along with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, to farm the land and harvest the crops. This farming would supply food and support for Mephibosheth's household and dependents. Mephibosheth himself would live at the court and eat his daily meals with the king.

Ziba agreed to obey every command the king gave him. Mephibosheth was welcomed at David's table and treated with the honor and love given to the king's own sons. The disabled prince was effectively received into the royal family as an adopted son.

Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica, through whom the family line of Jonathan was preserved for generations to come. All who lived in Ziba's household became workers dedicated to supporting Mephibosheth. The household of Saul was now secure and cared for under the king's protection.

Mephibosheth moved away from his place of hiding to live in Jerusalem, eating daily at the king's table. The passage ends by reminding the reader that he was crippled in both feet. David's grace gave him a completely new standing and royal honor, even though his physical weakness remained.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest David had mixed political motives, keeping Mephibosheth in Jerusalem under close royal surveillance to prevent any rival political rebellion.
